newsitem.title: CANADA: To connect or not to connect.
newsitem.headline: To connect or not to connect.

text.p: The majestic lighthouse that used to guide boats through the strait of Mississagi in Lake Huron is now only open for tourists.

The lighthouse, like many of its counterparts throughout Canada, has been replaced by a little beacon that flashes unfailingly day and night. Tourists, however, can pay $1 to tour the old facility and even see the quarters that housed the operators who kept it running it running 24 hours a day.

Lying in the crystal blue waters at the mouth of Georgian Bay, Manitoulin bills itself as the world's largest freshwater island and has retained much of its original charm as a spiritual haven for Canadian Indians and a farming and fishing settlement for European colonists.

I came here initially looking for a vacation to get away from it all; an "unplugged" kind of week away from televisions, telephones and computers. After scouring newspaper ads and talking to friends, I ironically found my one-week dream vacation spot on -- you guessed it! -- the Internet.
I stumbled upon CottageLINK (www.cottagelink.com), which displays a range or cottages for sale and rent throughout Canada, and to a lesser extent, in the United States and Mexico.

From there, I found Gerry Mack who with his wife and two kids run Viva Villa, a collection of four cottages, each named after animals such as "Fawn" and "Beaver." The pine cottages are filled with rustic but comfortable furniture and are literally a stone's throw from the clear waters of the island's Lake Kagawong.

I was able to arrange the cottage entirely by e-mail, except that I still had to use old-fashioned methods to send a deposit because Mack had not yet moved to e-commerce. At the Viva Villa, Gerry told me he didn't like to surf the Internet when he was on the island because he was encumbered with a slow 1,200-baud modem and would face long-distance charges because he did not have a local Internet service provider.

He didn't want the bother of getting a new one on the island, although he could have done that because the drugstore in the nearby town of Gore Bay was advertising immediate Net hookups with local access.

(As well he was probably just too busy to be lollygagging on the Net, what with regular maintenance and the need to chase down certain unamed renters who took a spin on the lake in another person's motorboat.)

The cottage was just what I had been looking for: it had the right amount of necessary electrical appliances, such as a coffee machine. There were no telephones or televisions, although the radio came in handy for weather reports when a rather impressive thunderstorm rolled in across the lake one evening.

Three young boys in tow, however, were not so enamoured with the idea of being without their favourite shows for a week. They maintained that position right to the end, but I don't think they realised how well they did without it. One son devoured an old copy of "Tom Sawyer" found in Gerry's shop, while the other two also read, drew pictures and discovered board games.

But I guess I did not do as well. I didn't bring my trusty laptop and as a result there were some withdrawal symptoms. Newspapers were hard to get on the island and many a time I wouldn't have minded zooming to my favourite news sites to find out what was going on. Not that I missed much: I Later found out that the "highlight" of the week was that some guy bit off an ear in some boxing match in Las Vegas.
I also often thought it would have been nice to catch up on my personal correspondence via e-mail while looking out across the lake from the knotty pine dining room table.

But, funny thing, when I got back to my beloved machines with multiple browsers and a couple of e-mail systems with more than 250 electronic messages, I realised again that being unplugged for a while was not all that bad.
Perhaps I could get a job in that lighthouse for a few months each summer. But then again with satellite communications on the way, maybe I could still bring the laptop ...
(For ideas or comments on the weekly Plugged In column contact: russell.blinch@reuters.com.)
